Cellphone Marketing

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa is in the top five in the world in numbers of spam phone calls. Without a workable recourse to control who can call you out of the blue, consumers are at the end of their tether.

Unique Selling Point:
Along with actual recordings of spam calls and vox pops we will approach the story with entertaining dramatizations to bring home the central point of the story, to show real live scenarios which random spam calls can negatively impact, for the sake of an unwanted call. Interviews will highlight the lack of recourse to stop this happening and how the Consumer Protection does very little presently but the new POPI Act, when enact, should change how the industry operates and is regulated.

Summary:
Many South Africans Endure a barrage of calls from business entities marketing numerous products to them. Information Sharing is a staple amongst big corporations in South Africa with or without the consent of the consumer. Consumers in South Africa usually just wish the calls away or try to block them, but there seems to be no recourse for the Business entities as they continuously taunt consumers.

Further information:
South Africa is in the top five in the world when it comes to the amount of spam calls local consumers receive. This is according to the "Truecaller Insights Top 20 Countries Affected by Spam Calls in 2017" report, which showed SA was in fifth place when it comes to the number of spam calls users get each month. With Financial services and Insurance companies representing a big chunk of that.


Certain do’s and don’ts apply when it comes to direct marketing practices in South Africa, which are regulated by the Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008 (CPA) and the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 25 of 2002 (Ecta). In terms of the CPA, direct marketers may market their products and services to consumers until they choose to optout. The permission of consumers is not required for a business to contact consumers telephonically and send emails or SMSs. Ecta, however, requires marketers to inform consumers of their right to optout of these communications.

However even with establishments such as the National Consumer Commission, consumers seem to have nowhere to turn to when facing a barrage of calls.

The Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (Popi), which aims to protect the privacy of consumers and their personal information, has been signed into law, but is not yet fully in operation. According to Lucien Pierce from PPM Attorneys specializing in Consumer Law, the prospect of this act coming into full effect has prompted a rush in information sharing as Corporations try to have as much consumer information as they can on their database and do as much telemarketing as possible while they still can.

Popi distinguishes between existing customers and new customers when considering the requirement to obtain consent for direct marketing practices. Opt-out consent will be required for existing customers, while opt-in consent will be required for new customers. Under the Popi Act, sending SMSs, emails and other electronic communication to potential clients will require these persons to first consent to it being sent as required by Popi, before you may contact them.

Nonetheless Consumers are today still required to give a tick of consent when they fill up a document or getting into a business- consumer relationship and even though they always tick “NO”, their information is still shared and they get harassed. Will the POPI Act be enough? Carte Blanche Investigates.

Along with actual recordings of spam calls and vox pops we will approach the story with entertaining dramatizations to bring home the central point of the story, to show real live scenarios which random spam calls can negatively impact, for the sake of an unwanted call. Interviews will highlight the lack of recourse to stop this happening and how the Consumer Protection does very little presently but the new POPI Act, when enact, should change how the industry operates and is regulated.

Press Release:


South Africa is in the top five in the world in numbers of spam phone calls. Without a workable recourse to control who can call you out of the blue, consumers are at the end of their tether.
We all loath those persistent telemarketing calls offering anything form insurance policies to cellphone contracts. Locally, it’s big business and when it comes to marketing phone calls, South Africa now ranks among the top 5 most spammed countries in the world. But is it legal to offer unsolicited credit or to keep your private contact details on a database after you’ve asked for it to be removed? Carte Blanche finds out what your rights are as a consumer.

Script:


Dramatisation – Emergency services, ambulances etc.... guy answers call sorry I'm in an emergency please call me later...
Medic: Hi… (Phone rings) Hello Denver speaking… No I don’t need an Insurance quote thanks. I’m just busy with a patient now. Can you call me back later?.... No I don’t need a quote now…. Sorry about that sir.

LINK: It's happened to most of us, when you get that inconvenient unwanted marketing call and in many professions most people are compelled to answer their phones in case of an emergency. South Africa is one of the.... (Interruption ring ring.... Hello, no.... you're not serious, really??? You're calling me now? To sell me something.... I'm actually quite busy at the moment ...bye... I said bye... Don't call me again!!!! )
As I was saying.. South Africa is ranked top five in the world in numbers of spam phone calls according to a True Caller report in 2017.

VO: Lucien Pierce a consumer Protection Lawyer says the public does have some recourse.

Lucien Pierce: There’s a law that dictates how people may use your personal information. Section 11 of the consumer protection Act, regulates direct marketing. It says that you can tell a direct marketer not to use your information, if they’ve gotten hold of it in a way that you haven’t agreed to. It also deals with what we would call a “do not” call database where you can register yourself on that database and then you may not be approached in any way by any direct marketers if you are on that database.

VO: And opt out is what most of us want, the people we spoke to feel harassed by the barrage of calls they get on a daily basis.

Macfarlane: How do you feel about getting those calls?

Vox Pops: Irritated. It’s frustrating, because irrespective of whether you’re working or not working they still go on with the call.

Vox Pops: Most of the time, the timing of all of it and they never give you the time for them to hear you that are you busy or not

VO: We wanted to track one of these telemarketing calls and it didn't take long for us to get one

Telemarketer: Sir I’m calling you with regard to our VIP status card which you been pre-approved for…

Thabo: Where do you get my details from?

Telemarketer: You’ve been spotted as a traveller and a credit card holder sir.

Thabo: I’m not a credit card holder

Telemarketer: If you’re not a credit card holder, you are a traveller.

Thabo: yeah everybody travels. Where do you get my info?

Telemarketer: Remember, we’ve got a database.

LINK: With or without your consent, telemarketers have all your information. Your cellphone, address, where you work and much much more. Where do they get this information if you never gave it to them?

Dramatisation: phone rings
Clement: Clem plumbing hello…No sorry, sorry I’m actually very busy right now… By the way where did you get my number?

VO: We have become targets to all forms of spam marketing be it phone calls, sms, or email. Gary Meiring is a data specialist and in the business of buying and selling personal information.

Gary: We source data from many different areas. We get feedback from some call centres where data comes back to us to confirm that it was correct data. But that would only be data that’s related to contact, public information. We used to have a telephone book. Everyone’s name and number and street address was in the telephone book.

Lucien: There will be a distinction between the two types of information you are talking about. Somebody who picks up a telephone directory and calls you, that is public information and it’s out there. But if a retailer compiles a database and on that particular database you’ve refused for your information to be used and it is then passed on to somebody else, they would be doing something illegal.

LINK: According to the consumer protection Act, all it takes to stop receiving a call from a certain marketer is simply to optout and your problems are solved. But how easy is it?

VO: We managed to get hold of the company that called us earlier to see if we could get off their database.


Cell phone footage Thabo calling back

Thabo: Hi how are you? … I’m alright. I just spoke to a colleague of yours who was trying to transfer me to sales, but the line dropped. I’m trying to find out where you guys get my information.

15:32 (phone rings) Line Cuts

22;17 Telemarketer: Hi sir did the call go through?

22:19 Thabo: No it didn’t

22:22 telemarketer: Ok I will try again. Please hold on

22:23 Thabo: No but then what if it happens one more time?

35:34 Thabo: see I’m not trying to….hello….fuck

49:56 telemarketer: She is one of our new consultants so she might have said something out of proportion. She is still learning. I have to apologise for that.

56:40 Thabo: Can you remove me please from your database?

56:42 telemarketer: I will send you an email confirming that.

VO: That process took us one hour. Not many people can afford to waste time removing themselves off databases they haven't consented to.

The Protection of Personal Information Act or POPIA was promulgated in 2013 but has yet to be enacted into law, once it is enforced it will change the way the Direct Marketing Industry operates.

Lucien: What the PoPi Act is going to do is that it provides that a cold caller may call you once. If you say “I’m not interested. Do not ever call me again” The law says that they may never ever call you again

VO: The National Consumer Commission is responsible for implementing and policing the laws that affect the direct marketing industry with regards to the Consumer Protection Act, Thezi Mabuza is the deputy Commissioner.

Thezi: When we have evidence to say that somebody has actually informed to desist and then they kept on doing that, what the Act allows us to do is to actually go and apply for a fine. The tribunal can issue a fine of up to a Million of their annual turnover or 10%, whatever is greater.

VO: And of course there are those even more frustrating automated calls like this one...

Thezi Listening to call..

Automatated call: Hello, do you have loans. Store accounts or other debts? Then this is for you.

Thezi: If it’s an Automated, it is very difficult sometimes because the number is even spoofed. For you to say who has called you and how do you opt out because already as you can see you are talking to a recorded message. What you can do is simply really to kind of like opt out.

VO: David Dickens CEO of Direct Marketing Association South Africa, says that some companies are trying to cash in before the new law takes effect.

David Dickens: The PoPi Act does not allow for computerised calls. Until the regulator takes office, there is that window and I see they are flogging that window

VO: The Industry is flooded and over saturated with a limited pool of consumers to sell to, and with such negative responses from people one wonders why telemarketing is such a popular form of getting products out there.

Gary: The percentages call centres sometimes work on, the conversion rate is sometimes as low as 0.8%. The Call centre business is a numbers game. The more calls you make, the more success you’ll have.

Macfarlane: What are some of the ones you usually get calls from?

VOX POPS: Mostly phone companies and insurers and loans.

Sound Up call centre Agent: Sir you are speaking to

VO: Carte Blanche visited a busy call centre in Randburg, to get a peek at the other side

Call Centre agent: There was a customer that told me I should …. I can’t use those words, but he told me how to get the short end of the stick

LINK: The direct marketing and telesales business is a multimillion rand industry in South Africa, creating employment for thousands of people, especially the youth. With the incoming POPI Act how will this affect them.

Call centre Manager: To be honest, it’s not entirely gonna affect our business, because we are practicing to be in line with the code of conduct in line with the POPI Act, but it is gonna mitigate these fly-by-night call centres

David: Already we’re sitting in a recession. In fact 26% of our industry is made up of youth and that’s going to be close to half a million. They’ll lose their jobs.

Thezi: What the regulation is doing is only setting out the rules on which how everybody within that industry, whether they belong to a association or not ought to be conducting themselves.

Macfarlane: So you’re saying people’s jobs are safe?

Thezi: People’s jobs are safe.

LINK: The direct Marketing association of South Africa is a body that regulates direct marketers, but only those that are affiliated to them. Once you put yourself on their “do not Call List” none of their members are allowed to call or market to you.

David: We’ve created a platform and we said you are all welcome to complain. We can take our members to task and there is a fine. Those that fall under outside our ombud will go to the NCC.

VO: A National central database where you have asked to opt out of whatever form of direct marketing you have agreed not to receive, would make sense and it has been in the offing for a number of years, so why has it not yet been implemented?

Thezi: For us on our side we have a clause and a mandate actually that allows us to setup an Optout registry and that is a mandate, which for now based on the constraints in the fiscus it has not been funded.

Macfarlane: How much are we looking at?

Thezi: We were looking at funding of roughly something below R80 Million. Because we needed a start up capital which is what we don’t have now.

VO: So it seems that while we wait for the POPI act to come into full fruition with an appointed regulator, the National Consumer Commission, the body entrusted to execute the outcomes of the act, will be rendered toothless in implementation without the necessary funding and in the meantime consumers have to continue being frustrated.

Dramatisation: Clem the plumber bursts the tap.

FIN

PROMO 1: 15”

VO: Telemarketing is big business in South Africa. Some people report multiple calls daily. Is it legal?

Lucien: What the POPI act is going to do is that it provides that a cold caller may call you once


PROMO 2. 15”

VO: We’ve all experienced the frustration of a telemarketing call, but what is even more annoying, is where do they get our details?

Gary: It will only be data that’s related to contact. Public information. We used to have a telephone book. Everyone’s name and number and street address was in the telephone book.


PROMO 10”

VO: Most call centres claim to remove you from their database when you are not interested in their products, but is there recourse when they don’t keep their promise and the calls keep coming?

metadata.Summary: Many South Africans Endure a barrage of calls from business entities marketing numerous products to them. Information Sharing is a staple amongst big corporations in South Africa with or without the consent of the consumer. Consumers in South Africa usually just wish the calls away or try to block them, but there seems to be no recourse for the Business entities as they continuously taunt consumers.
metadata.Further information: South Africa is in the top five in the world when it comes to the amount of spam calls local consumers receive. This is according to the "Truecaller Insights Top 20 Countries Affected by Spam Calls in 2017" report, which showed SA was in fifth place when it comes to the number of spam calls users get each month. With Financial services and Insurance companies representing a big chunk of that. Certain do’s and don’ts apply when it comes to direct marketing practices in South Africa, which are regulated by the Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008 (CPA) and the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 25 of 2002 (Ecta). In terms of the CPA, direct marketers may market their products and services to consumers until they choose to optout. The permission of consumers is not required for a business to contact consumers telephonically and send emails or SMSs. Ecta, however, requires marketers to inform consumers of their right to optout of these communications. However even with establishments such as the National Consumer Commission, consumers seem to have nowhere to turn to when facing a barrage of calls. The Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (Popi), which aims to protect the privacy of consumers and their personal information, has been signed into law, but is not yet fully in operation. According to Lucien Pierce from PPM Attorneys specializing in Consumer Law, the prospect of this act coming into full effect has prompted a rush in information sharing as Corporations try to have as much consumer information as they can on their database and do as much telemarketing as possible while they still can. Popi distinguishes between existing customers and new customers when considering the requirement to obtain consent for direct marketing practices. Opt-out consent will be required for existing customers, while opt-in consent will be required for new customers. Under the Popi Act, sending SMSs, emails and other electronic communication to potential clients will require these persons to first consent to it being sent as required by Popi, before you may contact them. Nonetheless Consumers are today still required to give a tick of consent when they fill up a document or getting into a business- consumer relationship and even though they always tick “NO”, their information is still shared and they get harassed. Will the POPI Act be enough? Carte Blanche Investigates. Along with actual recordings of spam calls and vox pops we will approach the story with entertaining dramatizations to bring home the central point of the story, to show real live scenarios which random spam calls can negatively impact, for the sake of an unwanted call. Interviews will highlight the lack of recourse to stop this happening and how the Consumer Protection does very little presently but the new POPI Act, when enact, should change how the industry operates and is regulated.
